doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

chapter: Big breaks: New Wave, Maynard, Tony Bennett
title: The New Wave band: rehearsing, vocalist Barbie Rankin and Tommy Sapienza's charts
summary: In the seventies New Wave, a year of rehearsing and writing charts with a scat vocalist, was a first big break.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I remember just the whole night. I can still see that room right now, yeah. Things like that, I just never ever forget. Plateaus. When you crack those certain plateaus, you never forget it. At least I haven’t. I can remember all the points where I found out the switch — I just moved a level. And this was my first one, to play a solo that I felt like appropriate, imaginative and the whole bit, and even the cats that night, I mean just when the set was over they were all like, oh man. You were burning, man. I walked out of there, like I keep using the analogy that it’s like when you get out of confession. That feeling that you have when you walk outside and everything smells fresh, and everything looks good. That’s the kind of feeling that I had. When I walked out that door it was like — cool man, I’m a player man. And the first big break: see I don’t know whether you equate the big breaks to the big name people or whether you equate them to circumstances and things that had an important impact on your life. The first big break. When I was with the New Wave, actually the New Wave was a big break. That was a band in the seventies. And all we did for a year that I was with them was rehearse, write new tunes, new charts, play the stuff that Tommy Sapienza wrote for us, and we had a vocalist that could scat great, Barbie

Rankin. She could scat great, sang really well, and would learn her parts just like any other horn player would. And we started doing like Ella charts, all these hip things, the stuff from Nancy Wilson/Cannonball Adderley.

Yeah. We started doing all those charts. Sap wrote them all out. And then I started, myself and Dave Javonne, when he was with us, another saxophone player here in Buffalo, started transcribing some of the tunes from Phil Woods’ albums and we’d write out his solo and then give it to her to learn. And then we’d write them in three parts and then we’d have alto, tenor and vocal, and we’d play them; or we’d do just like John Dankworth and Cleo Laine, where you play the unison line with the scatted vocal. And then we started doing flute on top. And we were like grooving. I mean we were really like looking for it. Long hangs at the house every night ‘till eight in the morning rapping about jazz, doing everything else. All the big jazz players that would come into town ended up over the house for a hang, and we were working a lot. And we would actually move a grand piano to our gigs when we got them. We had a Baldwin baby grand that Tommy had, and we’d have it moved. And that’s if we had — most of the gigs were six nights a week then. If we had more than two weeks we would move the piano at our expense. We had our own tuner that would come it and the whole bit.
